children: The U.K. government presents its annual budget later this month, but may find it difficult to reassure bond investors that it can lower its debts even if an independent watchdog judges that it remains on track to stick to its self-imposed rules.

The path to bringing borrowing down already requires tight limits on spending toward the end of this decade. But the jump in energy prices since the start of the war between the U.S. and Iran has increased the cost of providing public services, so the current spending allocations won't do as much as intended.

That has already blown the government off course. Its spending in the first five months of the fiscal year was 7.4 billion pounds ($9.79 billion) above the Office for Budget Responsibility's March forecast, with the result that borrowing was 8.1 billion pounds higher than targeted.

"For plans to reduce borrowing and meet the fiscal rules to be credible, the chancellor must set out overall spending envelopes that he would be genuinely prepared to live within," said Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies. "Simply penciling in implicit cuts that he has no intention of delivering would make the budget a work of fiction."

The stakes for the Oct. 28 announcements have increased over recent weeks as yields on government bonds have surged. Those moves largely reflect an increase in expected inflation as the Iran war drags on with no apparent end in sight. But they are also a response to growing worries about the ability of governments to contain a steady rise in their debts this century, and particularly this decade.

Even those governments that can claim to have laid out a path to reducing their debts face increased skepticism, a reflection of the fact that their predecessors have more often than not strayed when they have come under political pressure.
"The need of the hour is for credible medium-term fiscal consolidation plans," said Kristalina Georgieva, managing director of the International Monetary Fund, in a speech last week.

The U.K. government's budget plans are guided by two targets, one of which requires it to pay for day-to-day spending entirely out of tax revenues and borrow only to fund investment by the fiscal year ending at the start of April 2030.

The key metric for judging whether the government is likely to stick to its targets is the so-called headroom it has to meet that goal. In March, the OBR judged that it would reach its goal with 24 billion pounds to spare.

Since then, the war raised the day-to-day cost of running the government. At the same time, the increase in bond yields and higher inflation means the cost of paying interest on the government's debts has risen.

That combination will reduce the headroom. But it may largely be offset by a rise in tax revenues that is also linked to the war. Higher prices boost revenues from taxes on the sale of goods, services and assets, as well as taxes on profits and incomes.

As a result, the IFS--a nonpartisan research body that focuses on the budget--estimates that the government's headroom will likely be little changed at around 20 billion pounds. On the face of it, that should reassure bond investors, although other economists have lower estimates and the IFS acknowledged that there is a high degree of uncertainty about the final figure.
However, higher prices pose questions about whether the government will be able to stick to its path with the next election due to take place by late 2029 and possibly sooner.

If they were unchanged despite the rise in costs, the spending plans would imply cutbacks in the services provided by the government. Investors may question the plausibility of a budget that envisages cuts to public services that are timed to take place just as the government prepares to be judged by voters.
"Fiscal policy must be seen by markets as credible," Bank of England Gov. Andrew Bailey warned in a speech last week.

For now, France and to a lesser extent the U.S. appear to be the focus of attention in the market for government bonds, since they have larger budget gaps than the U.K., and lack a clear plan for reducing borrowing. Tweaking its plans to boost its credibility would help the U.K. government stay out of the crosshairs.

"This budget comes at a moment when the wary eyes of global financial markets are elsewhere," said Jack Meaning, chief U.K. economist at Barclays. "One of the chancellor's key priorities should be to keep them there."
